Will the eventual wording and scope of any reform be broad and unambiguous enough that the forecasting question would resolve as a clear 'increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years,' rather than being too partial, conditional, or category-specific to count?
A) Yes. Any reform that is passed will be framed broadly enough to clearly count as increasing the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years.
B) No. Any reform is likely to be partial, conditional, or limited to certain visa categories, making resolution as a clear yes doubtful.

Can the qualifying period for settlement be increased to 10 years through a mechanism that is politically and administratively feasible within the time window before May 2026?
A) A 10-year settlement qualifying period can be implemented through feasible rule changes within the available time.
B) A 10-year settlement qualifying period cannot be implemented feasibly within the available time because of political, legal, or administrative constraints.

Is there a clear political commitment from the government in power before May 2026 to extend the standard settlement qualifying period to 10 years?
A) Yes. The governing party will make a specific and credible commitment to a 10-year settlement period, making implementation more likely.
B) No. There will be no specific, credible commitment; politicians may discuss tougher migration policy without committing to a 10-year settlement rule.

Would any change, if adopted, apply broadly enough to count as the UK increasing the qualifying period for settlement, rather than only affecting narrow visa categories?
A) The reform would apply to the main settlement pathways broadly enough that the UK would clearly be judged to have increased the qualifying period for settlement.
B) Any eventual reform would be narrow, partial, or route-specific, creating ambiguity and making it less likely to count as a general increase in the settlement qualifying period.

Will increasing the settlement qualifying period to 10 years be a sufficiently high political priority, relative to other migration measures, that ministers devote scarce legislative/regulatory time to it before May 2026?
A) Yes. Ministers will treat this as a major deliverable on immigration and move it ahead of competing priorities.
B) No. Other migration or domestic priorities will crowd this out, leaving insufficient time or attention for enactment before May 2026.

Will any major pre-May-2026 settlement reform actually set the main qualifying period at 10 years, rather than preserving 5 years for most routes, creating only limited 10-year categories, or merely proposing the change for later?
A) Yes. Forecasters on this side believe that if settlement rules are reworked, the reform will genuinely make 10 years the central threshold rather than only adjusting edge cases or publishing a consultation.
B) No. Forecasters on this side believe any reform before the deadline will likely be partial, deferred, route-specific, or only consultative rather than establishing 10 years as the main qualifying period.

Will the electoral and party-management incentives facing the government up to May 2026 favor a substantive tightening on settlement rather than caution to avoid backlash from business, universities, health/social care, or moderate voters?
A) Yes. The political payoff from appearing tougher on long-term migration and integration will outweigh opposition from affected sectors or centrist critics.
B) No. Economic and political costs—especially employer, sectoral, and moderate-voter backlash—will push the government toward softer or more ambiguous approaches.

Will immigration policy priorities between now and May 2026 remain focused on visible restriction measures rather than shift toward other issues?
A) Immigration politics will continue to reward restrictive symbolic and substantive measures, keeping this reform near the top of the agenda.
B) Political attention will shift to other priorities, causing this proposal to lose momentum or be deprioritized before implementation.

Will the policy, if pursued, be applied broadly enough across major migrant routes that most forecasters/resolvers would judge that the UK has in fact 'increased the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years'?
A) Yes. The eventual reform will cover enough of the main routes to settlement that it will clearly count as an increase to 10 years in ordinary and market-resolution terms.
B) No. Any adopted measure will likely be partial, route-specific, heavily grandfathered, or framed differently, creating a real chance that it does not meet the forecast’s threshold.

Is current expert understanding of the baseline settlement regime accurate enough that forecasters are not confusing citizenship residence periods, long-residence rules, temporary visa routes, and ILR qualifying periods?
A) Yes. The forecaster correctly understands the current ILR framework and is not mixing up adjacent immigration concepts.
B) No. Many forecasters are likely mistaken about the baseline system, overstating how novel or feasible a '10-year settlement' change is because they conflate different residence rules.

Will the election and any change of government increase rather than reduce the chance of this specific reform being adopted before May 2026?
A) Yes. The post-election political configuration is at least as favorable to the reform as the pre-election one, or an incumbent government acts before leaving office.
B) No. The election or change of government lowers the chance sharply, with the incoming government shelving or reversing the idea.

Will the government in power before May 2026 prioritize migration restriction strongly enough to push through this specific change?
A) Yes. The governing party sees migration reduction as a top priority and is willing to spend political capital on this reform.
B) No. Other issues will crowd it out, and migration policy energy will go to more visible or easier measures instead.

Can the qualifying period for settlement be increased to 10 years through an immigration rules change or other executive action without requiring primary legislation that would materially slow or block implementation?
A) Yes. The government can do this mainly via immigration rules or secondary instruments, so implementation is procedurally feasible on a short timeline.
B) No. A durable change would require primary legislation, extensive legal work, or more procedural steps than expected, making the timeline too tight.

Is there likely to be political continuity—especially no change in governing priorities so large that the reform is dropped or delayed before May 2026?
A) Yes. Political control and policy direction will stay aligned with a tougher migration agenda long enough for the change to happen.
B) No. Political change or shifts in governing strategy will interrupt or reverse momentum toward this specific reform before May 2026.

Will political incentives before May 2026 favor a tougher legal-migration stance strongly enough that ministers prioritize this settlement change?
A) Political incentives before May 2026 will strongly favor prioritizing a tougher settlement rule.
B) Political incentives before May 2026 will not be strong enough to make this settlement change a priority.

Are legal, administrative, or political obstacles likely to delay or water down any announced settlement reform before May 2026?

B) Legal challenge risk, administrative burdens, interdepartmental disagreement, or electoral turnover will delay, dilute, or block the reform before May 2026.

Will any settlement reform adopted before May 2026 specifically set the standard qualifying period at 10 years, rather than merely tighten settlement rules in some other way?
A) If settlement policy is tightened before May 2026, the reform will specifically set the qualifying period at 10 years.
B) Any settlement tightening before May 2026 will take some form other than setting a universal 10-year qualifying period.

Can the UK legally and administratively implement a 10-year settlement qualifying period before May 2026 without delays from consultation, parliamentary process, operational complexity, or court challenges?
A) Yes. The government can make the change quickly, likely through Immigration Rules or related executive action, and any legal or administrative obstacles are manageable within the timeframe.
B) No. Even if discussed, the change faces meaningful procedural, legal, operational, or transitional hurdles that make implementation before May 2026 unlikely.

If ministers decide they want a 10-year settlement rule, can they implement it before May 2026 through powers and procedures that are practically available on that timeline?
A) Yes. The executive has enough control over immigration rules/policy instruments that, if politically chosen, the change can be made on this timeline.
B) No. Even if ministers support the idea, the needed rulemaking, consultation, parliamentary handling, operational prep, and policy design will make implementation before May 2026 unlikely.

Will external shocks or migration-related events materially raise the salience of toughness on immigration and accelerate policy implementation before May 2026?
A) Yes. Events such as high net migration figures, asylum controversy, or renewed political pressure make tougher immigration action more urgent and increase the odds of implementation.
B) No. Salience does not increase enough, or other events dominate; without a forcing shock, the policy remains one proposal among many and never reaches implementation.

Is there, before May 2026, a concrete government-backed proposal or decision to move the standard settlement qualifying period to 10 years, rather than only rhetoric or external speculation?
A) Yes. A specific, government-owned plan emerges—through a manifesto, ministerial announcement, white paper, or draft Immigration Rules—showing genuine intent to raise the settlement qualifying period to 10 years before May 2026.
B) No. No concrete government proposal materializes; discussion of a 10-year period remains speculative, rhetorical, or confined to leaks, commentary, or nonbinding party talk.

Is there a genuine and live UK government policy commitment before May 2026 to increase the standard qualifying period for settlement to 10 years, rather than merely discussing tougher migration controls in general?
A) Yes. There is or will soon be a concrete commitment by government leadership to this specific change, making action before May 2026 a serious live possibility.
B) No. General pressure for lower migration will not crystallize into a definite commitment to this exact settlement change before May 2026.

Will there be major elite or stakeholder resistance inside government or from business, higher education, or affected sectors that is strong enough to delay or block the change?
A) No. Internal and external opposition is limited, fragmented, or politically ignorable, so it does not stop the reform.
B) Yes. Significant pushback from departments, employers, universities, coalition factions, devolved actors, or other stakeholders helps stall, dilute, or abandon the policy.

Are transitional protections for people already on existing 5-year routes likely to be limited enough that a policy enacted before May 2026 would still count as increasing the qualifying period to 10 years in a meaningful way?
A) Transitional protections are likely to be narrow enough that the enacted policy would meaningfully establish a 10-year qualifying period rather than preserving the 5-year route for most affected people.
B) Transitional protections are likely to be broad enough that any near-term reform would leave most existing 5-year routes effectively intact, so it would not meaningfully amount to a broad increase to 10 years before May 2026.

Can the relevant change to the settlement qualifying period be implemented primarily through secondary instruments or Immigration Rules without requiring new primary legislation?
A) Yes. Ministers can implement the relevant change largely through Immigration Rules or delegated powers, so the institutional hurdle is comparatively low.
B) No. A durable or broad 10-year settlement change would require primary legislation or other slower processes, raising the hurdle materially.
